name: Candomblé
areas: the region where Candomblé coalesced in the 19th century; Salvador is sometimes called "Black Rome" and 1,144 terreiros were recorded there in 1997
the first terreiros opened in the late 19th century in a city then expanding rapidly
Afro-Brazilian migration brought a rapid rise: from virtually no terreiros until the 1960s to over 4000 by the end of the century
routes: Candomblé spreads from Bahia to Rio de Janeiro (late 19th century)
Growing emigration from Bahia carries it to São Paulo (20th century)
marks: By the founding myth, the Ilê Axé Iyá Nassô Oká was founded here in 1830 as the first terreiro.
Brazilians took part in the first International Congress of Orisha Tradition and Culture here in 1981.
The second International Congress of Orisha Tradition and Culture was held in Salvador in 1983.
notes: Candomblé coalesces in Bahia in the 19th century from the religions of enslaved Yoruba, Fon and Bantu people and Roman Catholicism; the first terreiro, by the founding myth, is founded in Salvador in 1830.
The constitution of 1891 enshrines freedom of religion, although the Penal Code of 1890 prohibited talismans and much herbal medicine and authorities shut down terreiros.
Candomblé becomes increasingly public in the 1930s, and a decree under President Vargas recognises the legitimacy of terreiros.
Migration from Bahia brings a rapid rise of Candomblé in São Paulo, and groups form abroad.
Brazilians take part in the first International Congress of Orisha Tradition and Culture in Ifẹ, Nigeria (1981); some practitioners try to remove Roman Catholic elements.
Evangelical Protestant opposition grows in the 2000s, including attacks on terreiros, and Candomblecistas respond with protest marches.
